transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Thank you for seeing me. I've been struggling a lot at work lately because in long meetings, people will talk directly to me and I just completely zone out. I only realize afterward that I didn't actually hear what they were saying, and it's getting really embarrassing.
Can you tell me more about what happens when you 'zone out' - do you feel like you're still in the room but just not hearing, or do you feel like you're somewhere else entirely?

I'm physically right there and usually looking directly at the person, but my mind has completely drifted off to mundane things, like planning what to make for dinner. Then I suddenly snap back and realize I didn't process a single word they said, leaving me completely unable to repeat it back.
When you 'zone out' and your mind drifts off, do you ever experience any feelings of detachment from yourself or your surroundings, as if you're observing things from outside your body?

No, I don't feel detached from my body or like I'm observing things from the outside at all. When I zone out, my mind is just drifting to ordinary, everyday thoughts like what to make for dinner, rather than feeling disconnected from reality. It's really just a case of my attention wandering off to mundane things.
Have you ever experienced any episodes where you felt like you were in a daze or a trance, or had significant memory gaps for events that occurred, beyond just zoning out in meetings?

No, I've never experienced any trances, dazes, or actual gaps in my memory. It's strictly that my focus slips and my mind drifts off to other topics during those long, dry meetings. I'm always fully aware of where I am, I just struggle to pay attention.

Do you find it difficult to sustain attention in other areas of your life, such as reading, watching TV, or during conversations with friends and family, or is this primarily a problem in work-related settings like meetings?

It's definitely not just at work, although that's where it causes the most professional stress. At home, I really struggle to sit still and pay attention when watching a movie or trying to relax with my partner in the evenings. I get this wired, restless feeling inside that makes it hard to focus, and it's actually starting to strain our relationship.
Do you often find yourself acting on impulse, doing things without much thought, like interrupting others, blurting out answers, or engaging in reckless behaviors?

I definitely struggle with verbal impulsivity, though I don't do physically reckless things. In meetings, I often blurt out answers before someone has even finished asking because I think I know where they're going, which means I miss important details. I also catch myself interrupting colleagues, finishing their sentences, and jumping into conversations, only realizing afterward from their reactions that I've overstepped.
Can you tell me more about this 'wired, restless feeling' you mentioned, such as whether it leads to fidgeting, an inability to sit still, or feeling constantly on the go?

Yes, if I sit still for more than 30 minutes, I get this wired, crawling feeling inside that makes me constantly jiggle my leg, click my pen, or find excuses to get up from my seat. It feels like I'm constantly on the go; my colleagues even joke about me pacing the halls, and I find it almost impossible to just sit and rest.

Do you often feel like you're driven by a motor, where you have to keep moving, and is this feeling present in both your work and personal life, making it hard for you to engage in leisure activities quietly?

Yes, I constantly feel like I'm driven by a motor. At work, colleagues joke that I can't sit still because I'm always pacing and starting new tasks, and at home, I end up reorganizing things instead of resting. It makes quiet activities like watching a movie with my partner feel almost unbearable, giving me a wired, crawling feeling that is really straining our relationship because I can't just relax.
Can you describe how often these symptoms of inattention, impulsivity, and restlessness occur, and have you experienced them consistently across your life, or have they developed more recently?

While these issues have really come to a head over the last two years since my company's restructuring forced me into this meeting-heavy role, they aren't entirely new. Looking back, my elementary school teachers always wrote on my report cards that I couldn't sit still, talked over classmates, and was constantly sent to the hallway, even though I was smart and did well on tests.
Have you noticed any patterns or triggers that make your symptoms of inattention, impulsivity, and restlessness better or worse, such as time of day, environment, or specific situations?

They are definitely much worse during long, back-to-back meetings, structured presentations, or budget reviews where I'm required to sit still for more than 30 minutes. Conversely, I do much better with dynamic, project-based work and quiet analysis where I can move around freely and organize tasks around my own rhythms.

You mentioned that your teachers noted these behaviors in elementary school; did you experience significant difficulties with attention, impulsivity, or restlessness during adolescence and young adulthood as well, or did these issues become more pronounced in recent years?

I'm not entirely sure, as I haven't thought about that period in my life very much. While I definitely had those issues in elementary school, I think I managed to get by through high school and college, and it wasn't until the recent major restructuring at work that things became truly difficult.

Can you clarify whether you believe these symptoms of inattention, impulsivity, and restlessness have been present and caused significant impairment consistently throughout your life, or if they have significantly worsened in recent years, particularly in relation to the changes in your work environment?

The tendencies have definitely been there since childhood, like when my elementary school teachers complained I couldn't sit still or wait my turn, but they didn't cause major impairment until recently. It was really the restructuring at work two years ago, with all the long, back-to-back meetings, that brought things to a head and made them highly disruptive to my career and personal life.
